summary: Documents how BGP-4 met the requirements for advancing a routing protocol to Draft Standard, reporting experience with the protocol. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This report records how BGP-4 worked in networks in the mid-1990s. It describes implementations, deployment experience, migration, and issues that remained open.

questions: how did bgp-4 reach draft standard
subtitle: A 1995 report on BGP-4 implementations, deployment, and unresolved issues.

tldr.problem: Advancing BGP-4 required evidence that it met the routing-protocol standardization criteria, including independent implementations and operational experience.
tldr.mechanism: The memo reports implementation and production experience, the transition to classless routing, and open questions about metrics, internal peering, and routing changes.
tldr.outcome: It documents interoperable implementations and broad use among significant autonomous systems at the time, while identifying areas for further work. It is Informational and obsoletes RFC 1656.

today: RFC 1773 is an Informational report published in March 1995 that obsoletes RFC 1656. Its operational observations describe BGP-4 at the time of writing; the unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates this report.

sections.title: Purpose of the Experience Report
sections.content:
RFC 1773 documents how BGP-4 met the requirements for advancing a routing protocol to Draft Standard. It is the second of two reports; the companion report provides a performance analysis.

The memo discusses the general requirements and Draft Standard requirements in the routing protocol criteria. Its evidence comes from implementation and operating experience with BGP and BGP-4.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo presents evidence that BGP-4 met specified criteria for advancing a routing protocol. It reports on implementation and use rather than defining a new protocol.

sections.title: Changes Across BGP Versions
sections.content:
BGP is an inter-autonomous-system routing protocol for TCP/IP networks. Version 2 introduced path attributes and removed relationship types used in version 1. Version 3 changed use of the NEXT_HOP attribute and added a BGP Identifier to the OPEN message.

BGP-4 replaced class-based network reachability with prefixes of arbitrary length. It also changed AS-PATH to describe sets of autonomous systems and added the MULTI-EXIT-DISCRIMINATOR, LOCAL-PREFERENCE, and AGGREGATOR attributes.
sections.plainLanguage: BGP changed through several versions. BGP-4 let one routing entry describe prefixes of different lengths and added routing attributes.

sections.title: Implementations and Network Use
sections.content:
The report names five independent implementations in the operational Internet: Cisco Systems, the gated consortium, 3COM, Bay Networks, and Proteon. It says implementing BGP-4 took about two person-months on average, not counting work to support CIDR.

BGP had been used in production since 1989 and BGP-4 since 1993. The report describes a varied environment, from links of 28 Kbits/sec to 150 Mbits/sec, and reports that the largest backbone had nearly 90 BGP speakers. The carried exterior routes numbered well over 20,000 aggregate entries.
sections.plainLanguage: Several independent teams built implementations that interoperated. The report also describes BGP-4 operating across different network sizes, link speeds, and routing arrangements.

sections.title: Moving to Classless Routing
sections.content:
BGP-4 was deployed while routing tables were growing rapidly and placing demands on memory and processor capacity. Operators tested it on a virtual network linked through tunnels before enabling it on production equipment.

During the transition, BGP-4 routers negotiated BGP-4 with each other and used BGP-3 with older peers. After testing, some sites withdrew class-based advertisements and used CIDR aggregates, encouraging other transit providers to migrate, accept a default route, or lose access to some destinations.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators tested BGP-4 before using it in their production networks. During the changeover, newer routers could still communicate with older BGP-3 peers.

sections.title: Issues the Report Leaves Open
sections.content:
The report describes the MULTI-EXIT-DISCRIMINATOR as a weak metric used late in path selection among external peers in the same autonomous system. LOCAL-PREFERENCE lets an operator override the default path choice, but the report notes that a common default value would help multi-vendor routers within one system.

Other open topics included ways for a network to express transit preferences, the number of TCP connections needed for internal BGP in large autonomous systems, and whether route-damping methods should be required in future BGP-like protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: The report identifies work that remained open, including how to express transit preferences and how large networks should distribute routing information internally.
